title: White, red and black mountains
hookLine: mountains with streaks of white, red and black, and those with knowledge stand in awe (35:27–28)
last: HE ADDS TO CREATION AS HE WILLS.

lines: A ROAD CUT: ROCK IN BANDS.
cards: Drive through a road cut, where the highway slices straight through a hill, and you'll see it: the rock in bands. A pale stripe, a rusty red one, a dark one, stacked like a layer cake. Most people glance and keep driving.
A geologist pulls over. To her, each band is a chapter: mud, ash, iron and a long stretch of time. Surah Fatir points at exactly those stripes, and then says who, looking at them, feels the most awe.
It isn't the person you might expect.

teach.b: Verse twenty-seven asks: haven't you seen that Allah sends water from the sky, and with it brings out fruits of different colors? And in the mountains, streaks, white and red, of different hues, and others jet black.
The word for the streaks, judad, means tracks or paths, lines running through the rock. The word for the deepest black, gharabib, is linked in the dictionaries to ghurab, the raven.
Verse twenty-eight keeps going: and people, and animals, and cattle, also of different colors. A whole palette, from fruit to stone to faces. Then the line the passage was building to.
Pickthall: "The erudite among His bondmen fear Allah alone."

teach.h: THOSE WHO KNOW STAND IN AWE.
teach.b: The Arabic word is al-'ulama', those who know. Today it usually means religious scholars, and many read the verse that way. But notice where it sits: right after rocks, rain, fruit, animals and human skin.
Some commentators point out that the knowledge here can include knowing creation, looking long enough at the stripes in a mountain to be moved by them.
The verb is yakhsha, from khashya, a fear that's really awe: the trembling respect of someone who understands how great a thing is. Some people assume that the more you know, the less wonder is left.
The verse says the opposite: the ones who know are the ones who stand in awe.

how: Muslim scholars often cite 35:28 to describe the link between learning and reverence, and many Muslims count reflecting on creation (tafakkur) as a form of worship.

games.q: colors and knowledge — tap the pairs.

s: the verse says knowledge drives out wonder
it says the opposite: those who know stand in awe of Allah.
the passage lists colors in fruit, mountains, animals and people
verses 27–28 move from fruit to rock to living things.
the colors in the mountains are white, red and black
streaks white and red, of different hues, and others raven-black.

games.q: the verse has just described colored mountains, animals and people. who does it say truly stands in awe of Allah?
games.why: al-'ulama', those who know. placed right after the colors of creation, some commentators include knowing the world itself.

practice: Find a stone, from a garden, a sidewalk, a windowsill, or a countertop if that's what you have, and hold it close, looking for colors you missed at first: a vein, a speck, a band.
Turn it over, and think about how long it took to become what it is. If no stone is near, look at the back of your own hand the same way.

wordCard.voice: White. The first color named in the mountains' streaks in Surah Fatir: white, red and raven-black, a palette the verse says moves those who know to awe. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: white (plural), the first color of the mountains' streaks in 35:27.

carryVoice: Your line: knowledge brings awe. White, red, and raven-black. Tomorrow, the heart of the book.
